title: Beijing's Central Axis Is Not a Relic but a City Operating System Still Running
dek: The Ming rebuilt Beijing from a blueprint written two thousand years earlier, and the central axis still dictates the symmetry and growth of a city of twenty million — even the Olympic Bird's Nest sits on that line.
why: Medium information density, but its strength is restoring the central axis from a tourist sight to a planning logic still in effect — suited to anyone interested in cities and organizational design.
who: Founders, product leads and investors interested in urban planning, organizational design and institutional continuity; especially good for the commute.

points.h: A manual from two thousand years ago is still in use
points.body: When the Ming set out to rebuild the capital, they dug up a technical manual written more than two thousand years earlier, the Kaogong Ji (“考工记”). It specified a city four to five kilometers on each side, three gates per side, the palace at the center, an ancestral temple on one side, the court in front, the market behind, and a Temple of Heaven in the southern suburbs. The historian Jeremiah Jenik says the logic behind this layout was cosmic order: just as there is a fixed point in the sky, the North Star, there should be a corresponding fixed point on earth, and the most fitting fixed point was the emperor himself — placing himself in the palace at the exact center of the city was placing himself inside a cosmic order revolving around him.

points.h: They actually built it to the blueprint
points.body: The most astonishing thing is not that the Ming dared to use a blueprint over a thousand years old, but that they built so close to it. Overlay the Kaogong Ji plan on the model at the Beijing Planning Exhibition Hall and the two almost coincide. So Beijing today is still a twenty-first-century city running around a fifteenth-century heart, and that heart follows principles laid down nearly two thousand years ago. Compare London, which grew organically along the Thames: Beijing had the blueprint first, then the city.

points.h: The central axis is a spine, and the city grew out of it
points.body: From north to south, the central axis strings together the Bird's Nest, the Drum and Bell Towers, Jingshan, the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, and finally Yongdingmen at the southern end. The episode likens it to a spine: everything was planned and expanded outward from this line. Running due north-south and aligned with the heavens, this line has been Beijing's most distinctive feature for six hundred years, and it determines the shape of the city today.

points.h: The power to tell time is the power to rule
points.body: The Drum and Bell Towers were the timekeeping center of the entire city, and the bell was said to be audible twenty kilometers away. From 1272 all the way to 1924 — the year the last Qing emperor left the Forbidden City — the time struck here was Beijing's official time. The drum was beaten one hundred and eight times every two hours; it was the first sound Beijingers heard in the morning and the last they heard at night. The episode says it was almost as if the emperor were not merely marking time but claiming ownership of time itself.

points.h: Jingshan was piled up from the rubble of a previous dynasty
points.body: Jingshan is not a natural hill; it was artificially piled up by the Yongle Emperor according to feng shui principles. An ideal palace faces south, with water to the south that curves and flows to bring qi and vitality, and a mountain to the north to block evil influences from the north and display majesty. Beijing is too far from the Yan Mountains to the north, so the Ming used rubble from the old Mongol palaces and earth dug from new water channels to build a symbolic mountain inside the city.

points.h: The Forbidden City was a nationwide logistical megaproject
points.body: Ten thousand logs were shipped from 1,800 kilometers to the southwest, golden bricks from Suzhou 1,100 kilometers to the south — 18 million bricks fired in all — and gold leaf from Nanjing. One million laborers plus more than 100,000 craftsmen built it in fifteen years. From the 1420s to the early twentieth century, twenty-four emperors lived here. Today it receives more than 15 million visitors a year, making it the most visited historical site on earth.

points.h: A nail-free wooden structure can withstand a magnitude 9.5 earthquake
points.body: These buildings are almost entirely wood, and what lets them stand for centuries is the dougong (斗拱): the dou are the bearing blocks, the gong fit into them, and they interlock very tightly. Wood shrinks and warps, and this system allows it to deform flexibly while keeping the overall structure intact; during an earthquake every small piece of wood can slide a little, without shearing the bearing blocks or popping screws. Scientists have calculated that this construction could withstand the strongest earthquake ever recorded, magnitude 9.5.

points.h: It was struck by lightning within a year of completion
points.body: The Forbidden City was not fireproof. Less than a year after it was completed in 1421, the Three Great Halls were burned to ashes by a lightning strike. Afterward 308 bronze vats were installed to store water in case of another fire. This detail shows that even the most precise planning cannot prevent a single point of failure; it can only add redundancy after the fact.

points.h: An imperial procession could halt a city of a million
points.body: The winter solstice sacrifice to heaven was the most important ritual in the entire Chinese calendar. The emperor went south from the Forbidden City along the central axis, then turned toward the Temple of Heaven. The proceedings were extremely solemn: commoners had to close their windows, and no one was allowed to see the emperor pass; Beijing's newly installed tram system shut down entirely for the day; foreigners were explicitly told not to leave their homes and not even to steal a glance. A city of a million people ground to a halt for this.

points.h: A demolished gate was rebuilt exactly as it was
points.body: By the mid-twentieth century Beijing's population was approaching four million, and the city could no longer cope, so Yongdingmen was torn down to build a new ring road system. But the central axis needed an endpoint, so in the early 2000s Yongdingmen was reconstructed a few meters from its original site. The episode points out that the ring roads themselves became an extension of this symmetry — the first, the second, the third, ring after ring. A line drawn centuries ago still dictates the form of a twenty-first-century global metropolis.
